729.title: Karna's abandonment
729.hook: a son is born shining, in armor and earrings, and his young mother sets him on the river
729.carry: a person on each side of it
729.howItsDone: Some retellings of the Mahabharata, in storytelling, dance and theater, linger on Kunti at the riverbank, letting audiences sit with her grief rather than rushing past it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Karna's abandonment began: Pritha, Durvasa's mantra, and the sun answering a girl's curiosity. I only wanted to see if it worked.

A baby is born in secret, already dressed for battle. The Mahabharata says he's born wearing armor that's part of his own body, with bright earrings in his ears, shining like his father, the sun. Any newborn would be scandal enough for an unmarried girl in a king's house. This one glows. There's no hiding him in a corner. And his mother is still very young, still a daughter under her father's roof.
screen: `BORN IN SECRET.` → `ARMOR AND EARRINGS.` → `SHINING LIKE THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Kunti's choice is quick in the telling, and heavy in the hearing. Afraid of what her family and the world will say, she places her newborn son in a basket and sets it on the river. A later part of the poem tells the scene again at length: she weeps over the basket and speaks to the child, asking the gods of the waters, the sky and the earth to keep him safe, and saying that whoever finds him will be blessed to raise him. Then the current carries him away. Listen to the word the text chooses. It doesn't call her cruel. It calls her afraid, tells us why, and lets us watch her grief. Some readers hear a mother failing her child. Some hear a frightened girl doing the only thing she could see to do. Some hear both at once, and the poem seems to allow that. And notice the armor. The baby is sent off alone, but not unprotected. He's wrapped in his father's gift, and those earrings and that armor will matter enormously later. The word abandonment can sound like a verdict. In this story, it's also an event with a person on each side of it: a mother on the bank, a child on the water. The Mahabharata will follow both of them for a very long time.

730.title: Karna's abandonment
730.hook: a charioteer and his wife find a basket on the river, and raise the boy inside as their own
730.carry: let go upstream, taken in downstream
730.howItsDone: In retellings, Karna is also called Radheya, son of Radha, honoring the mother who raised him; listeners meet him under that name as well as Karna.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a shining baby in a basket, and a frightened mother blessing him from the bank. A person on each side of it.

Downstream, a man and his wife are by the water. He's Adhiratha, a charioteer, a suta, whose work is driving and caring for the chariots of warriors. She's Radha. The text tells us they have no child. Floating toward them comes a basket. They pull it to the bank, open it, and find a baby boy, glowing, in armor and earrings. Yesterday we stood with the mother who let go. Today we stand with the parents who catch.
screen: `DOWNSTREAM: ADHIRATHA AND RADHA.` → `A BASKET ON THE WATER.` → `A BOY INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Adhiratha and Radha take the boy home and raise him as their son. There's no long debate in the telling. They wanted a child, and here is one. They name him Vasusena, a name that points back to the armor and earrings he was born with. Later the world will know him as Karna. He's also called Radheya, son of Radha, after the woman who raised him, not the one who bore him. Hold onto that name. Here's what the river has done. Karna was born to a princess and a god, and has grown up in a charioteer's house. In the world of the Mahabharata, that matters. Birth decides a great deal: who may compete, who may rule, who gets laughed at. For most of his life Karna will carry royal blood he doesn't know about, and a charioteer's home he will not disown. Both will be pressed on him by others, and both are part of who he is. Abandonment is only half of this story. The other half is adoption. A child let go upstream is taken in downstream, and Karna will carry both halves all his life: the loss from upstream, and the home from downstream.

731.title: Karna's abandonment
731.hook: the boy grows up worshipping the sun, and one morning a stranger asks him for the armor he was born in
731.howItsDone: In Hindu storytelling Karna's name is tied to giving: his gift of the armor to Indra is retold as a picture of keeping one's word to give, whatever it costs.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a charioteer and his wife caught the basket downstream. Let go upstream, taken in downstream.

Every morning the young man stands facing the sun, hands joined, praying, until the sun is high and its heat is on his back. That's Karna, grown. He doesn't know the sun is his father. And the text adds a detail: while he prays, there's nothing he will refuse a Brahmin who asks. Today a stranger comes during that hour, and asks for the one thing Karna was born wearing.
screen: `HE FACES THE SUN EACH MORNING.` → `WHILE HE PRAYS, HE REFUSES NO BRAHMIN.` → `A STRANGER COMES.`

segments.voice: The stranger is dressed as a Brahmin, a priest. But the Mahabharata lets us in on the secret: he's Indra, king of the gods, and the father of Arjuna. Indra knows that as long as Karna wears his armor and earrings, nobody can beat him, so he comes to ask for them as alms. The Adi Parva tells this scene early, beside Karna's birth, though in the story's order it comes years later. In a later book, the sun himself warns Karna in a dream that Indra is coming, and tells him to refuse. Karna answers that he can't. He's given his word to give, and he'd rather lose his life than his name for giving. So the Brahmin asks. And Karna takes a blade, cuts the armor from his own body and the earrings from his ears, and hands them over. Indra, the text says, is pleased, and gives Karna a weapon in return, a dart that can kill one enemy. Now set this inside our story. Karna was abandoned once, set adrift by a mother who couldn't keep him. The armor was the one gift from his father that went with him. And today he gives it away with his own hands. The poem doesn't stop to call it wise or foolish. It shows the blade, and the gift: the boy who lost so much at the start of his life chooses to lose more, because someone asked.

732.title: Karna's abandonment
732.hook: at the princes' tournament a stranger walks into the arena and matches Arjuna, and one woman in the stands knows him
732.howItsDone: The tournament scene, with Karna's entrance and Kunti's fainting, is retold by Mahabharata storytellers and on stage, where it lets the audience see what the characters can't.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a stranger asked for the armor, and Karna cut it from his body. He gives because someone asked.

Yesterday's scene came from further down the road; today we're back in the order of events, and Karna still wears his armor. A great arena in Hastinapura. Drona, the princes' teacher, has arranged a day for them to show the city what they've learned. The stands are packed, Kunti among the women. The cousins ride and fight and shoot, and Arjuna outshines them all, the text says, while the crowd roars. Then a sound at the gate. Someone new walks in.
screen: `A DAY TO SHOW THEIR SKILL.` → `ARJUNA OUTSHINES THEM ALL.` → `A SOUND AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: It's Karna, tall and shining, in his armor and earrings. He barely bows to the teachers. He turns to Arjuna and says, in effect: everything you've done, I'll do. And he does, one feat after another, while the crowd stares. Duryodhana is overjoyed. Here at last is someone to match the brother he resents, and he embraces Karna like a friend. Then Karna asks to fight Arjuna, one against one. And now the story swings up into the stands. Kunti sees the armor and the earrings, and she knows. This is her son, the boy she set on the river, about to fight another of her sons. The text says she faints. Vidura has her revived with cool water and sandal paste, and she comes to and watches, unable to say a word. Everyone else in the stands sees two rivals. One person sees two brothers, and she can't tell anyone. The abandonment wasn't only something that happened long ago by a river. It's still happening, in the silence of a mother in a crowd. Karna doesn't know. Arjuna doesn't know. Only Kunti does, and us, the listeners. Every word spoken in that arena now means two things.

733.title: Karna's abandonment
733.hook: asked who his father is, Karna has no royal answer; Duryodhana makes him a king, and an old charioteer walks into the arena
733.carry: it follows him into every room
733.howItsDone: In retellings, Karna's bow to Adhiratha in the arena is told as a sign of his loyalty to the father who raised him, and his friendship with Duryodhana is traced to this day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Karna matched Arjuna, and Kunti knew her son and kept silent. She can't tell anyone.

Two fighters are ready to face each other. Then Kripa, one of the teachers, steps between them with a question that sounds polite. Arjuna is a prince, son of Pandu and Kunti. Tell us your mother and father, your royal line. A prince fights only an equal. And Karna, who has just matched every feat in the arena, has no answer to give. The text says he lowers his face.
screen: `KRIPA ASKS FOR HIS LINEAGE.` → `A PRINCE FIGHTS ONLY AN EQUAL.` → `KARNA LOWERS HIS FACE.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana jumps in. If Arjuna will only fight a king, then let Karna be a king. And there in the arena he has Karna crowned king of Anga. Karna, overwhelmed, asks what he can give in return. Duryodhana asks only for his friendship, and Karna gives it. Then, through the crowd, comes an old man, trembling, his cloth slipping. It's Adhiratha, the charioteer who pulled a basket from the river. And Karna, the new king, his hair still wet from the crowning, bows his head to him and greets him as his father. Adhiratha holds him and weeps. It's the moment Bhima has been waiting for. You're a charioteer's son, he says, so pick up a whip; you're not fit to fight Arjuna, or to rule Anga. Duryodhana defends his friend: the origins of heroes, like the sources of rivers, are hard to know. Look at the armor and earrings this man was born with. Then the sun sets, and the day ends with nothing settled. Look at these six days together: a girl's curiosity, a basket, a charioteer's home, an armor given away, a mother's silent recognition, and now a crown and an insult on the same afternoon. Karna's abandonment isn't one event. It follows him into every room. And the thing held against him, his birth, is the one thing he doesn't know the truth of.

734.title: the lac house
734.hook: the city starts calling Yudhishthira its future king, and Duryodhana makes his father an offer: a holiday in Varanavata
734.howItsDone: The bait in this story is a festival of Pashupati, a name of Shiva; Hindus still worship Shiva as Pashupati, and the Pashupatinath temple in Kathmandu carries the name.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Karna's abandonment: a crown, a bow to the old charioteer, an insult at sunset. It follows him into every room.

Talk in the streets of Hastinapura: people are saying Yudhishthira should be king. He's fair, he's truthful, he's Pandu's eldest. Dhritarashtra is blind, so he was passed over before; why should his line rule now? Word reaches Duryodhana, and it burns. The Mahabharata gives him a long, anguished speech to his father: if Yudhishthira takes the throne, the crown will pass down his line, and we and our children will be shut out.
screen: `THE STREETS TALK.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA SHOULD BE KING.` → `DURYODHANA BURNS.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana's plan is dressed up as a kindness. Send the Pandavas away, he tells his father, to the town of Varanavata, where a festival of Pashupati, a name of Shiva, is under way. Let them enjoy themselves, out of the capital, out of the people's eyes. Dhritarashtra hesitates. Pandu was good to me, he says, and the people love his sons; how can I do this? But he loves his own son, and in the end he agrees. So the old king calls his nephews in and speaks warmly of Varanavata: a lovely town, a festival, go and enjoy it. Yudhishthira sees the purpose behind it, the text says, but he's alone and without friends at court, and he agrees. Then Duryodhana calls a minister named Purochana and gives him the real job. Go ahead to Varanavata. Build a fine house for the Pandavas, out of lac and resin and other things that burn, plastered over so it looks like any house. Treat them well. Earn their trust. And one night, while they sleep, set it on fire. Notice the shape of the plot. Nothing is done in the open. A father is persuaded, a holiday offered, a house built with care. Every step looks generous: a trap made of kindness. And it can't happen without the blind king, who hesitated, and then said yes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lac house was planned: a holiday offered, a blind king persuaded. A trap made of kindness.

A farewell at the edge of the city. The Pandavas and their mother are setting out for Varanavata, and an unhappy crowd has followed them out. Vidura, their uncle, walks beside Yudhishthira and says something strange, in a tongue the crowd doesn't understand, the text says, that only Yudhishthira can follow. To anyone listening, it sounds like a riddle. To Yudhishthira, it's a warning.
screen: `A FAREWELL AT THE CITY'S EDGE.` → `VIDURA SPEAKS IN A HIDDEN TONGUE.` → `A WARNING IN PLAIN SIGHT.`

segments.voice: Vidura's riddle goes something like this. There's a weapon not made of steel that can still destroy a body; whoever knows it can't be killed by it. A fire that burns a whole forest can't reach the creatures that live in holes underground. Someone who knows the roads, who can find the way by the stars, will survive. Fire, holes, roads, stars. Yudhishthira answers simply: I have understood. Later, on the road, Kunti asks what all that was about, and he tells her: Vidura was warning us of fire. Then they arrive. Varanavata welcomes them with joy. Purochana greets them warmly, and after some days moves them into the new house. Walking through it, Yudhishthira catches a smell: fat, and lac. He turns to Bhima. This house, he says, is made to burn. Now step back and look at the week. Karna gave away his armor. He walked into an arena where only his mother knew him. He was crowned and mocked in a single afternoon. Then a plot was laid, and a warning given in words no one else could read. A week of hidden things: a hidden brother, a hidden grief, a hidden trap, a hidden message. The Mahabharata keeps letting the listener in on secrets the characters don't share. Today, at least, one hidden thing is caught in time.
screen: `FIRE, HOLES, ROADS, STARS.` · `I HAVE UNDERSTOOD.` · `THE HOUSE SMELLS OF LAC.` · `A WEEK OF HIDDEN THINGS.` · then, large: `THIS HOUSE IS MADE TO BURN.`
